strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: unified representation learning for multivariate time-series foundation models across forecasting, imputation, and anomaly detection.

The proposed model combines several sensible ingredients, including patching/channel independence, decoder-only autoregressive generation, a GLM-inspired blank-infilling objective, and an FFT-based time-granularity conditioning mechanism.
The empirical scope is broad, covering multiple standard datasets and three generative task families, with some ablations for pretraining, frequency components, and time-granularity modules.
The manuscript provides useful implementation details for pretraining scale, model size, patching, optimizer, and hardware, making the high-level setup reasonably understandable.
weaknesses: The evaluation is not sufficiently controlled for a top-tier conference. Many comparisons are based on best reported numbers from prior papers or source code rather than a unified reimplementation under matched data splits, lookback lengths, tuning budgets, and fine-tuning protocols. This is especially problematic for foundation-model claims.

The central claim that time granularity is a crucial missing component is weakly supported. The KDE/FFT visualizations show that datasets with different sampling rates have different frequency distributions, but this is almost tautological and does not establish that the proposed attention mechanism learns transferable universal knowledge rather than exploiting dataset identity or sampling-rate metadata.

The novelty is incremental. The method combines known ideas from PatchTST-style patching, RevIN, decoder-only time-series models, FFT/frequency modules, and GLM-style blank infilling. The paper does not clearly isolate a technically deep new mechanism beyond a low-rank frequency adapter gated by time-granularity embeddings.

Ablations are incomplete. The paper ablates frequency and time-granularity components only on forecasting, not on imputation or anomaly detection, and does not disentangle the effects of model size, pretraining data volume, blank infilling, autoregressive generation, dynamic lookback selection, and the proposed Fourier knowledge attention.

Several reported gains are small or inconsistent. For example, pretraining improves traffic and electricity forecasting by around 0.5-1.2%, and anomaly detection by about 1.2 F1 on average. Some benchmark comparisons show GTM losing to simple or prior models on individual datasets, weakening the broad superiority claim.

There are table and reporting inconsistencies. In the imputation table, Electricity appears to have much better Informer numbers than GTM, yet the text says GTM is second-best or best except Electricity; the main table and appendix values appear inconsistent. Such issues undermine confidence in the experimental reporting.

The anomaly detection protocol uses point-adjusted F1, which is known to inflate performance and obscure practical detection quality. The paper does not report more robust metrics such as event-wise precision/recall, affiliation metrics, delay-aware metrics, AUC-PR, or results without point adjustment.

The paper claims no downstream customization, but the experiments still involve task-specific preprocessing changes, removal of masking/2D position encoding, omission of patching for imputation, thresholding for anomaly detection, and dynamic lookback selection. The distinction between no architecture change and no task adaptation should be stated more carefully.

Important baselines are missing or only partially included. Recent large forecasting foundation models such as TimesFM, MOIRAI, Lag-Llama, Timer, Time-MOE, and UTSD are discussed but not consistently evaluated across the main tasks, despite being central to the paper's positioning.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or pretrained model release is mentioned, hyperparameter search and fine-tuning details are sparse, statistical uncertainty is absent, and the compute cost is substantial. This makes it hard to verify the results or assess whether improvements come from the proposed method rather than tuning and scale.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: building a unified multivariate time-series foundation model that can support forecasting, imputation, and anomaly detection with minimal task-specific architectural changes.

The proposed combination of temporal attention, FFT-based frequency processing, and time-granularity conditioning is a plausible modeling direction, and the paper makes an effort to motivate it with empirical frequency-domain visualizations.

The experimental section covers several common benchmark families and includes some useful ablations, including pretraining vs. no pretraining and variants without the frequency/time-granularity modules.
weaknesses: The central novelty is overstated. Frequency-domain modeling, patching, channel independence, decoder-only pretraining, and reconstruction/masking objectives are all heavily explored in recent time-series work; the paper does not convincingly isolate what is fundamentally new beyond a relatively simple granularity-conditioned low-rank frequency module and an adaptation of GLM-style blank infilling.

The empirical claims are stronger than the evidence. The paper repeatedly claims GTM outperforms SOTA methods across all generative tasks, but its own tables show several cases where GTM is not best, e.g. forecasting averages against TTM/PatchTST on some datasets, imputation on Electricity, and anomaly detection on MSL/SMD/PSM.

Baseline selection is incomplete and inconsistently justified. Several highly relevant recent foundation models discussed in the related work, such as TimesFM, MOIRAI, Lag-Llama, Time-MOE, and other strong forecasting models, are not included in the main empirical comparisons. This makes the SOTA claims hard to accept.

The evaluation protocol is not sufficiently rigorous. Many baseline results appear to be cited from papers or source code rather than reproduced under a controlled setup, and the paper admits that aligning settings is difficult. This undermines fairness, especially for a large pretrained model compared against smaller or differently tuned baselines.

The anomaly detection evaluation relies on point-adjusted F1, which is known to inflate performance and can substantially distort conclusions. The paper does not report more robust anomaly metrics or sensitivity to thresholding, despite making broad claims about anomaly detection superiority.

The ablations are too limited to support the main causal story. The improvements from time-granularity and FFT components are often small, and there is no deeper analysis of whether gains come from model scale, pretraining data, masking strategy, Fourier module, time-granularity embeddings, or ordinary hyperparameter differences.

The pretraining benefit is modest in several settings, especially Traffic and Electricity forecasting and anomaly detection, which weakens the claim that the method learns broadly universal time-series knowledge.

The claimed empirical finding about distinct frequency-domain distributions across granularities is mostly descriptive. The paper does not establish that this observation is novel, statistically robust, predictive of downstream transfer, or specifically addressed by the proposed architecture better than simpler frequency/time-feature baselines.

Reproducibility is limited. Important details such as code availability, exact data filtering, train/validation/test splits for all settings, baseline tuning budgets, random seeds, variance/error bars, and compute comparison are either absent or insufficiently specified.

Presentation quality is below the standard expected for a top-tier venue. There are numerous typos, formatting issues, inconsistent table labels, unclear equations, and overbroad wording, which make the technical contribution harder to assess and reduce confidence in the experimental care.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: a unified foundation model for multivariate time-series generative tasks, including forecasting, imputation, and anomaly detection, without task-specific architectural changes.

The proposed GTM combines several sensible ingredients: decoder-only autoregressive modeling, blank infilling pretraining adapted from GLM-style objectives, temporal attention, FFT-based frequency processing, and explicit time-granularity conditioning.
The empirical scope is broad. The paper evaluates on standard forecasting, imputation, and anomaly detection benchmarks, and reports generally strong results across many datasets and horizons.

The ablation studies are useful: pretraining improves over training from scratch, and removing frequency/time-granularity components consistently hurts performance, supporting the main design choices.

The paper is well positioned relative to recent time-series foundation models such as Timer, UniTS, UP2ME, TimesFM, MOIRAI, and TTMs, and the motivation for task-agnostic generative adaptation is compelling.
weaknesses: The evaluation is not fully convincing as a top-tier foundation-model comparison. Many baseline numbers appear to be cited from papers or source repositories rather than reproduced under a unified protocol, which weakens claims of superiority, especially given different pretraining data, model sizes, fine-tuning budgets, and lookback-window choices.

The novelty of the empirical finding about time granularity is somewhat overstated. Different sampling granularities naturally imply different frequency resolutions and ranges after FFT, so the paper needs stronger statistical controls to show that the observed frequency-domain distribution differences are nontrivial and not mostly an artifact of sampling rate, scaling, normalization, or dataset/domain composition.

The proposed Fourier Knowledge Attention mechanism is plausible but under-analyzed. The paper does not deeply justify the specific five-granularity key design, low-rank module structure, or the additive global full layer, nor does it compare against simpler alternatives such as explicit sampling-rate embeddings, frequency-domain MLPs, or standard cross-attention over frequency features.

The anomaly detection evaluation relies on point-adjusted F1, a known optimistic metric that can substantially inflate performance. Results are also mixed: GTM is not best on several individual datasets, and gains over GPT4TS on average are small.

Some headline claims are stronger than the evidence. The model is described as a universal representation model, but evaluation is limited to generative tasks and excludes classification despite discussing it as a major MTS task category. The paper also does not convincingly demonstrate zero-shot or broad cross-domain transfer beyond fine-tuning settings.

Reproducibility details are incomplete for a foundation-model paper. The manuscript gives some training hyperparameters, but lacks parameter counts, training time, code/model-release information, sensitivity analysis, and a clear accounting of compute versus baselines.

The writing and presentation contain numerous errors and inconsistencies, including typos, table inconsistencies, missing MAE values for some baselines, repeated/mislabeled table entries, and unclear statements such as 'path' instead of 'patch'. These do not invalidate the work but reduce confidence in experimental care.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: building time-series foundation models that transfer across forecasting, imputation, anomaly detection, and classification.

The proposed architecture combines temporal attention with an explicit frequency-domain module conditioned on sampling granularity, which is a reasonable and potentially useful inductive bias for heterogeneous time-series data.
The experimental section is broad, covering multiple generative tasks, classification, zero-shot/few-shot settings, ablations, pretraining-size/model-size scaling, and efficiency measurements.

Results are often competitive, especially for imputation and several anomaly-detection metrics, and the appendix includes useful additional analyses such as confidence intervals and modern TSFM comparisons.
weaknesses: The central novelty is somewhat incremental. Fourier/frequency-domain modeling and masked/reconstruction pretraining are well explored in time-series models, while the paper does not clearly establish that its specific granularity-aware Fourier attention is a major conceptual advance over prior frequency-aware or universal TS models.

Several major claims are overstated. The claim of being the first generative-task-agnostic TSFM is not convincingly distinguished from TIMER, UP2ME, UniTS, MOIRAI-style models, and others; moreover, the method still changes preprocessing or heads in some settings, e.g. removing masking/2D positional encoding, omitting patching for imputation, and replacing the projection head for classification.

The evaluation is not fully controlled. Many baselines are cited from papers or source code rather than reproduced under matched data, tuning, compute, and pretraining conditions. The main table omits several recent strong TSFMs, and the appendix shows GTM losing clearly to Time-MOE/Sundial on ETTh1 while the paper still claims consistent SOTA performance.

Zero-shot evidence is mixed: GTM wins only on average under incomplete coverage, while it is substantially worse than TimesFM on ETTm1 and worse than TIMER on Traffic. This weakens the foundation-model/generalization narrative.

Ablation and pretraining gains are often small, particularly on Traffic and Electricity, and the scaling-law claim is not well supported by rigorous scaling analysis; the presented curves show modest monotonic improvements rather than a demonstrated scaling law.

Technical details of the Fourier attention are underspecified or potentially inconsistent, including complex-valued FFT handling, dimensional compatibility of the low-rank matrices, residual/normalization structure, and why five fixed granularity keys should generalize to irregular or mixed-frequency data.

Reproducibility is limited: the code link is blank, data filtering to prevent downstream leakage is asserted but not detailed enough, and important training/fine-tuning choices and baseline tuning protocols are not sufficiently specified.

The anomaly-detection evaluation relies partly on point-adjusted F1, which is known to inflate performance; the TSB-AD results help, but thresholding and protocol details remain too thin for strong confidence.

strengths: The paper addresses an important time-series foundation model problem: building a single model that can adapt across forecasting, imputation, anomaly detection, and classification settings.

The proposed use of frequency-domain processing with explicit time-granularity conditioning is a reasonable modeling idea, and the empirical observation that frequency/phase distributions vary by sampling granularity is potentially useful.
The manuscript includes a broad experimental suite across multiple task types, plus ablations, zero/few-shot comparisons, pretraining-scale analysis, and efficiency measurements.
The hybrid reconstruction/forecasting pretraining objective is simple and could be practically useful if validated under fair and reproducible settings.
weaknesses: The main claims are substantially overstated. The paper repeatedly claims SOTA performance and the first generative-task-agnostic TSFM, but the method still requires setting changes across tasks, fine-tuning, removal of masking/positional components, omission of patching for imputation, and a replaced head for classification. The novelty over prior masked reconstruction, autoregressive infilling, Fourier/time-series modules, and existing multi-task TSFMs is not convincingly established.

There are serious inconsistencies in the reported results. For example, the Electricity imputation numbers differ between the main table and the appendix; the appendix shows Informer far outperforming GTM, while the text claims GTM is second-best. This undermines confidence in the experimental reporting.

The evaluation is not sufficiently controlled. Many baseline results appear to be copied from papers or source code rather than reproduced under unified settings. The paper itself notes that aligning models is difficult, yet then makes strong SOTA claims. Important recent TSFMs are only partially compared, and in Table 20 Time-MOE/Sundial outperform GTM on ETTh1 while this is not reflected in the main narrative.

Several headline results are weak or selective. Classification performance is mixed, with GTM clearly underperforming on JapaneseVowels, PEMS-SF, Heartbeat, and SelfRegulationSCP1. Zero-shot comparisons average only over models with available entries and obscure cases where GTM is worse, such as ETTm1 versus TimesFM and Traffic versus Timer.

The anomaly detection evaluation relies on point-adjusted F1 in the main table, a known problematic protocol, and although TSB-AD metrics are added, the setup and thresholding details remain insufficient. The gains over GPT4TS/other baselines in the main anomaly table are modest and not clearly significant.

The technical description has unresolved issues: the Fourier attention equations are dimensionally and computationally unclear, especially regarding complex FFT outputs, low-rank frequency matrices, inverse FFT handling, and how the granularity query is represented and learned. The rank-1 module design also seems under-justified.

The ablations are too limited to isolate the claimed contributions. The paper lacks comparisons to simpler frequency-domain baselines, alternative granularity encodings, no-pretraining but matched-capacity variants, random/static granularity labels, and separate ablations for hybrid masking, span shuffling, 2D positional encoding, and tail masking.

The scaling-law claim is not supported. The model/data scaling experiments cover only a few small configurations and show relatively small improvements, which is far from demonstrating a scaling law in the foundation-model sense.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The code link is blank in the extracted manuscript, and many fine-tuning details, baseline configurations, model selection procedures, compute budgets, and statistical testing protocols are missing or vague.

The paper has clarity and polish issues, including duplicated text, grammar problems, inconsistent terminology, and table formatting errors. These presentation issues are not merely cosmetic because they coincide with substantive reporting inconsistencies.

strengths: The paper proposes a coherent and practically motivated time-series foundation model combining decoder-only temporal modeling with a granularity-aware Fourier attention module and a hybrid reconstruction/autoregressive masking objective.

The empirical scope is broad: forecasting, imputation, anomaly detection, classification, zero-shot/few-shot transfer, ablations, scaling with model/data size, and efficiency analyses are all included.

Results are generally strong across several standard benchmarks, especially imputation and multi-task generative settings, and the added comparisons to recent TSFMs such as Time-MOE and Sundial improve the credibility of the forecasting evaluation.

The paper includes useful component ablations showing gains from frequency-domain modeling and time-granularity modules, plus comparisons against non-pretrained GTM that support the value of large-scale pretraining.
The method is relevant to an active area, and the focus on generative-task-agnostic adaptation is a meaningful practical direction for time-series foundation models.
weaknesses: The central novelty is somewhat incremental: Fourier-domain modeling, patching, RevIN/channel independence, decoder-only backbones, and GLM-style blank infilling are all established ingredients, and the paper does not fully isolate why this particular combination is fundamentally new beyond engineering integration.

Some claims are overstated, especially 'first generative-task-agnostic TSFM' and broad scaling-law claims. The evidence shows improved performance with larger models/data, but not a rigorous scaling-law analysis.

Baseline comparability is uneven. Several main-table results are cited from prior papers or source code rather than reproduced under a unified protocol, and the appendix itself notes that aligning baselines is challenging. This weakens claims of consistent SOTA performance.

The strongest recent forecasting baselines are only partially covered in the main text; in the appendix, Time-MOE and Sundial outperform GTM on several ETTh1 metrics, so the main claim that GTM outperforms all SOTA models is too broad.

Anomaly detection results rely partly on point-adjusted F1, a known inflation-prone metric. The TSB-AD extension helps, but more detail on thresholds, validation use, and per-dataset variance would be needed for strong confidence.

The classification evaluation is relatively weak for a claimed general model: GTM modifies the output projection head, performance is mixed, and several UniTS entries are missing, making the discriminative-task evidence secondary.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the main text says code and implementation details are available but the code link appears blank in the extracted manuscript, and key details such as exact preprocessing, splits, hyperparameter selection per task, and pretrained checkpoint availability are not sufficiently clear.

Some improvements are modest on core forecasting datasets, and ablation gains are often small, raising the possibility that much of the performance comes from scale/pretraining and careful tuning rather than the proposed Fourier/granularity mechanism itself.
